notes.short: Two lines, two ways: the righteous and the wicked
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite. Both lines speak of a way: the LORD guards one, and the other perishes.

lines.words: For the LORD guards the path of the righteous,
but the way of the wicked will perish.

original.note: In Hebrew both lines use the same word, derekh, “way”; the BSB says “path”, then “way”.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) sets the way of the ungodly against the way of the righteous. Barnes calls verses 4 to 6 a strong contrast between the unrighteous and the righteous. Henry: the Lord approves the way of the righteous and is angry at the way of the wicked, which shall perish.

cites.quote: God knows this way, which on this very account also unfailingly reaches its goal. On the contrary, the way of the ungodly … perishes, because left to itself

notes.short: The godly man is “like a tree planted”
notes.about: The man who delights in the LORD's law is said to be like a tree planted by streams of water. It is set in place and watered, not left to grow wild, so it bears fruit in season and its leaf stays green. Verse 4 gives the opposite picture: chaff.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: like a tree planted by streams of water
figure.means: the man who meditates on God's word: rooted, fed by it, fruitful and lasting

original.note: In Hebrew “streams” is peleg, from a root meaning to divide: channels or brooks that carry water.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Simile: the man who meditates in God's word is planted and protected like a tree in a garden. Henry calls it a similitude, the rivers being the means of grace; Barnes, a beautiful image of a tree set out with care where its roots have water; Delitzsch says God's word is to that man what the brook is to the tree.

cites.quote: Here, the similitude tells us that the man who meditates in God’s word is planted and protected, just as a tree in a garden is cared for as a “tree of the field” is not.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: His blessedness is here illustrated by a similitude ... He shall be like a tree, fruitful and flourishing. ... That he is placed by the means of grace, here called the rivers of water

notes.short: The wicked are “like chaff driven off by the wind”
notes.about: The wicked are likened to chaff, the light husk the wind blows away when grain is winnowed. Set against the planted tree of verse 3, the picture shows them without root or fruit, of no worth, and soon swept away.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: like chaff driven off by the wind
figure.means: the wicked: without root or fruit, worthless, and soon gone

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Simile and calls the contrast between the driven chaff and the planted tree most striking and solemn. Barnes says the winnowed chaff pictures the worthlessness of the wicked; Delitzsch: without root below or fruit above, worthless and unstable; Henry: of no worth in God's account, with no solidity.

cites.quote: The contrast between the driven chaff and the “planted” tree is most striking and solemn. The two comparisons are the great features of the Psalm

cites.quote: are the opposite of a tree planted by the water-courses ... without root below, without fruit above, devoid of all the vigour and freshness of life ... thus utterly worthless and unstable.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: whereas the righteous are like valuable, useful, fruitful trees, they are like the chaff which the wind drives away ... notes.short: The Lord “laughs”: His scorn told in human terms
notes.about: The One enthroned in heaven laughs at the rulers who plot against the LORD and His Anointed. Laughter is spoken of God in human terms, to show His contempt for their vain plans. It can also show His calm as He carries out His own. Psalm 37:13 speaks of His laughter in the same way.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.words: laughs
figure.means: God's contempt for the rulers' vain plotting against Him and His Anointed

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia, among the human actions spoken of God, as laughing. Clarke calls the words spoken after the manner of men, for utter contempt of their efforts; Barnes says the same, and that God goes calmly on with His purposes and looks on their efforts with contempt; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a bold figure, the laughter of supreme contempt.

cites.quote: Laughing. ... “He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord ... shall have them in derision.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Will smile at their vain attempts; will not be disturbed or agitated by their efforts; will go calmly on in the execution of his purposes. ... notes.short: God's “fingers”: the heavens are His own handiwork
notes.about: David calls the heavens the work of God's fingers, speaking of God as a craftsman working with his hands. The picture shows the heavens as God's own direct work; it can also speak of the skill and the ease with which He made them.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.words: the work of Your fingers
figure.means: God's own direct act in making the heavens, which can also speak of the skill and ease of His work

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia: a finger is given to God for the putting forth of His power to form, His own direct act. Albert Barnes says fingers may point to skill rather than strength. Henry says God made the heavens easily, with no outstretched arm, and with fine care, as an artist works with his fingers.

cites.quote: A Finger is attributed to God, to denote the putting forth of His formative power, and the direct and immediate act of God.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The work of thy fingers - Which thy fingers have made. The fingers are the instruments by which we construct a piece of work - perhaps indicating skill rather than strength; and hence so used in respect to God, as it is by his skill that the heavens have been made.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: They are therefore his, because they are the work of his fingers. He made them; he made them easily. The stretching out of the heavens needed not any outstretched arm; it was done with a word; it was but the work of his fingers. He made them with very great curiosity and fineness, like a nice piece of work which the artist makes with his fingers.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The LORD pictured as a shepherd caring for his flock
notes.about: David calls the LORD his shepherd. The picture shows God’s care for His people: He feeds, leads and guards them as a shepherd does his flock, so they lack nothing they truly need. Jesus later says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: The LORD is my shepherd
figure.means: the LORD, who feeds, leads and guards His people as a shepherd does his sheep

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Metaphor: the LORD is shown as a Shepherd who tends His people. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a metaphor from pastoral life for God’s care; Calvin, the similitude of a shepherd; Henry says David, once a shepherd, illustrates by it God’s care of His people; Barnes calls it a comparison that speaks of tender care and protection.
notes.limit: Some of the writers also see Christ in this Shepherd, pointing to John 10; the note claims only the picture of the LORD’s care.

cites.quote: Here, we have a Metaphor; and in it a great and blessed truth is set forth by the representation of Jehovah as a Shepherd. It is He who tends his People, and does more for them than any earthly shepherd does for his sheep
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Under a metaphor borrowed from scenes of pastoral life, with which David was familiar, he describes God's providential care in providing refreshment, guidance, protection, and abundance
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Under the similitude of a shepherd, he commends the care which God, in his providence, had exercised towards him. His language implies that God had no less care of him than a shepherd has of the sheep who are committed to his charge.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Time was when David was himself a shepherd; ... so he knew by experience the cares and tender affections of a good shepherd towards his flock. ... By this therefore he illustrates God's care of his people

notes.short: As a deer longs for water, so the soul for God
notes.about: The psalmist likens his longing for God to a thirsty deer that pants for streams of water. The picture shows how strong his desire is to come before God again, as the next verse asks, “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?”

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You
figure.means: the soul’s strong longing for God, like a thirsty deer’s longing for water

original.note: In Hebrew the same verb, arag, is used of the deer and of the soul; the BSB says “pants”, then “longs”. The deer longs for water below it, the soul for God above.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse among the similes built on as and so. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the poet compares his soul’s thirst for God to a stag’s, the hind’s longing going down, the soul’s up. Henry: he compares it to the panting of a hart. Barnes calls it an image of the earnest longing of a soul after God; Clarke likens the spent hart to the psalmist panting for God.
notes.limit: Some writers picture the deer as hunted and spent; the verse itself speaks only of its longing for water.

cites.quote: The hart panting, and the soul longing (Psa 42:1 (2)).
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The poet compares the thirsting of his soul after God to the thirsting of a stag. ... על and אל point to the difference in the object of the longing, viz., the hind has this object beneath herself, the soul above itself
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He compares it to the panting of a hart, or deer, which is naturally hot and dry, especially of a hunted buck, after the water-brooks. Thus earnestly does a gracious soul desire communion with God
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Nothing could more beautifully or appropriately describe the earnest longing of a soul after God, in the circumstances of the psalmist, than this image.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The hart feels himself almost entirely spent; he is nearly hunted down; the dogs are in full pursuit; he is parched with thirst; and in a burning heat pants after the water ... Thus pursued, spent, and nearly ready to give up the ghost, the psalmist pants for God, for the living God!
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: David's tears kept in God's book
notes.about: David says his tears are already in God's book. A book is a human thing spoken of God: it tells that He has noted every tear and will not forget them. The bottle beside it pictures the same care.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.words: Your book
figure.means: God's sure remembrance of David's tears, spoken of as a record He keeps

original.note: In Hebrew the last words, in Your book (sifrah), take up the first verb, taken account of (safar), so the verse ends where it began.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists this verse under Anthropopatheia, where a book is attributed to God. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the verse figuratively sets forth that God gathers His saints' tears as in a bottle and notes them as in a memorial (Malachi 3:16); he ties the last words to the first verb. Henry and Barnes read the book as God's book of remembrance: the tears are recorded, not forgotten.

cites.quote: A Book is attributed to God. … A Book of Life

cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: God has a bottle and a book for his people's tears, both those for their sins and those for their afflictions. … That he will remember them and review them, as we do the accounts we have booked.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: In thy book of remembrance; are they not numbered and recorded so that they will not be forgotten?

notes.short: “Righteousness and peace have kissed” like friends
notes.about: The psalm speaks of loving devotion, faithfulness, righteousness and peace as if they were persons. Two meet together and two kiss, as friends do. The picture shows them joined in full harmony, with none at odds with another.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed
figure.means: these four, pictured as friends who meet and kiss, joined in full harmony

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a charming allegory: mercy meets fidelity like one guardian angel meeting another, and righteousness and peace kiss like two inseparable brothers. Barnes: they kiss as estranged friends do when made friends again, blending in harmony. Henry, among other readings, takes the kiss as the harmony of God's mercy and truth, righteousness and peace, in salvation.
notes.limit: The writers agree on the picture, not on where the meeting is found: in God's renewed blessing on His people and their land, or in the salvation Christ brings, where mercy and justice agree.

cites.quote: The possessions that make a people truly happy and prosperous are mentioned under a charming allegory ... Mercy or loving-kindness walks along the streets of Jerusalem, and there meets fidelity, like one guardian angel meeting the other. Righteousness and peace or prosperity, these two inseparable brothers, kiss each other there, and fall lovingly into each other's arms.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Have kissed each other - As friends and lovers do ... but they have been now united as separated and alienated friends are, and have embraced each other as such friends do; that is, they blend together in beautiful harmony.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Of the harmony of the divine attributes in the Messiah's undertaking. ... God's mercy and truth, and his righteousness and peace, have kissed each other; that is, the great affair of our salvation is so well contrived ... that God may have mercy upon poor sinners, and be at peace with them, without any wrong to his truth and righteousness.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Three lines that climb as the floods rise
notes.about: Each line goes a step further: the floods have risen, then raised their voice, then lift up their pounding waves. The first two lines tell what has happened, and the third what is happening still. The next verse answers that the LORD on high is above them all.

lines.words: The floodwaters have risen, O LORD;
the rivers have raised their voice;
the seas lift up their pounding waves.

original.note: In Hebrew all three lines use the same word, rivers, which the BSB gives as floodwaters, rivers and seas, and the same verb, lift up. The first two verbs tell what has happened; the third tells what goes on still.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the thought is unfolded across the lines, the first two verbs telling what has taken place and the third what is still taking place. Henry reads the floods lifting up their voice as terror, and then their waves as real danger, and verse 4 as the anchor in that storm: God is on high, above them.

cites.quote: These rivers … have lifted up, have lifted up their murmur, the rivers lift up their roaring. The thought is unfolded in a so-called "parallelism with reservation." The perfects affirm what has taken place, the future that which even now as yet is taking place.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A threatening storm supposed: The floods have lifted up, O Lord! (to God himself the remonstrance is made) the floods have lifted up their voice, which speaks terror; nay, they have lifted up their waves, which speaks real danger. … The Lord himself is mightier. Let this keep our minds fixed, (1.) That God is on high, above them
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Rivers clap their hands, mountains sing
notes.about: The psalm calls the rivers to clap their hands and the mountains to sing, as people do for joy. With the sea and the world, all creation is called to rejoice before the LORD, who comes to judge the earth (verse 9). Isaiah 55:12 and Psalm 96:11-12 have a like picture.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: Let the rivers clap their hands, let the mountains sing together for joy
figure.means: the joy of all creation before the LORD, shown as if rivers and mountains could rejoice as people do

notes.evidence: Bullinger calls verses 7-8 a beautiful example of Personification, stressing the joy of the whole creation. Albert Barnes reads it as if the rivers were conscious and joined the praise. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): nature shares man's joy, high waves meeting like clapping hands. Henry and Benson: the floods rejoice as men do when they clap their hands, Henry adding, if they could.

notes.short: Lightning and clouds frame hail and snow
notes.about: The first four things named, which come down from the sky or rise toward it, can be read in a crossing order: the first answers the last, and the middle two answer each other. So lightning goes with clouds, and hail with snow.

lines.words: lightning
and hail,
snow
and clouds,

original.note: In Hebrew the first and last of the four are fire and smoke, which the BSB gives as lightning and clouds; the middle two are hail and snow.

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the four, which come down from heaven or rise toward it, are arranged after the model of a chiasmus, a crosswise order, so that fire and smoke answer each other, and hail and snow.
notes.limit: Other writers take the four as two pairs in the order they are named, lightning with hail and snow with clouds, or group the clouds with the hail and snow as water in the sky. The crossing is one writer's reading.

cites.quote: Then to four phenomena of nature, coming down from heaven and ascending heavenwards, which are so arranged in Psa 148:8, after the model of the chiasmus (crosswise position), that fire and smoke ... hail and snow stand in reciprocal relation
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Walk, stand, sit: three steps further into sin
notes.about: The verse climbs in three steps: the blessed man does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, stand in the path of sinners, or sit among mockers. Each step goes further, from taking their advice to keeping their way to settling among scoffers, and many see the men grow worse at each step too.

lines.words: who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked,
or set foot on the path of sinners,
or sit in the seat of mockers.

original.note: In Hebrew the three verbs are walk, stand and sit; the BSB gives the second as “set foot.”

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anabasis: evil counsel is taken, then carried out, then settled in as on a seat. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) finds a climax in the three names for the wicked; Barnes a double climax in nouns and verbs, Clarke in the three characters and in walk, stand and sit. Calvin puts the seat at the top of the climax; Henry traces the steps to the height of impiety.
notes.limit: All the writers see the verse climb, but they place the climb differently: in the three names for the wicked, in walking, standing and sitting, or in counsel, path and seat. One doubts that the names rise, except for the mockers.

cites.quote: Here is a triple Anabasis depending on Parallelism … Again, the first continue in that mind, taking evil counsel. The second carry it out, as the principle of their walk. The third settle down in their evil, as on a seat.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The three appellations form a climax: impii corde, peccatores opere, illusores ore … Therefore: Blessed is he who does not walk in the state of mind which the ungodly cherish, much less that he should associate with the vicious life of sinners, or even delight in the company of those who scoff at religion.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: We have here, then, a beautiful double gradation or climax, in the nouns and verbs of this verse, indicating successive stages of character. cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The nations rage, the peoples plot
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. The peoples can be taken as the nations of the first line, seen in the same uproar, and what they plot will prove vain.

lines.words: Why do the nations rage
and the peoples plot in vain?

the Lord taunts them.

notes.short: Seven lines open with “The voice of the LORD”
notes.about: Seven times a line begins with the same words, “The voice of the LORD.” They name the thunder and roar of a great storm, heard as God’s own voice, and their return line after line is the heart of the psalm.

The voice of the LORD is powerful;
the voice of the LORD is majestic.
The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars;
The voice of the LORD strikes with flames of fire.
The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness;
The voice of the LORD twists the oaks and strips the forests bare.

original.note: In Hebrew the phrase is two words, qol YHWH. Qol, voice, is used of any deep, rumbling sound, such as thunder.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists these verses, where the voice of the LORD begins seven clauses in a row. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the chief matter with the poet is the sevenfold voice of the LORD, the deep rumbling sound by which God makes Himself heard. Barnes notes that the phrase is seven times repeated in the psalm and refers to thunder, in which it seems as if God spoke.
notes.limit: The voice is chiefly the thunder of the storm; it can also take in the roar of the tempest and the quaking of the earth.

notes.short: The floods rise, then roar, then pound

the seas lift up their pounding waves.

notes.short: A question that says no one can praise Him enough
notes.about: The psalm asks who can tell all the mighty acts of the LORD or give Him all the praise He is due. The answer it expects is no one: His deeds are greater than any words. Some add that this is a reason to praise Him all the more, as best we can.

the LORD opens the eyes of the blind,

the LORD loves the righteous.

praise Him for His excellent greatness.

notes.short: His sanctuary is His mighty heavens

Praise Him in His mighty heavens.

figure.words: How long, O LORD, how long?
figure.means: the unfinished end of his prayer: how long he must suffer, and how long before the LORD rises to help him

notes.about: The three lines say one thing three ways: if I am guilty, let my enemy bring me down to death. Read this way, my honor is David himself, his soul and life of the lines before. The lines can also be read as going a step further each time, down to the dust.

may he trample me to the ground
and leave my honor in the dust.

original.note: In Hebrew the three lines name my soul, my life and my honor, or glory; the BSB gives me, me and my honor.

notes.about: The second line asks the first question again in other words: man becomes the son of man, and being mindful of him becomes caring for him. Both lines marvel that God takes thought for one so weak, with nothing in him to earn such honor.

or the son of man that You care for him?

notes.about: In Hebrew this psalm is set out in the order of the alphabet, though the order is handled freely and not carried through in full. Psalm 10 shares the pattern, and the two psalms can be read as a pair. A poet can use the letters in this way to express his feelings to the full.

figure.name: Acrostic
figure.words: I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart;
figure.means: This line opens the psalm, which in Hebrew is set out in the order of the alphabet, an order handled freely and not carried through in full.

notes.short: A lion, then a young lion: one picture twice

like a young lion lurking in ambush.

notes.about: David pictures his danger as torrents that overwhelm him. When he cries out, the LORD comes down in a storm, with earthquake, thunder and lightning, and draws him out of deep waters. Verse 17 says it plainly: “He rescued me from my powerful enemy.” The same song is in 2 Samuel 22.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: He drew me out of deep waters
figure.means: God’s rescue of David from foes too mighty for him (verse 17), pictured as a drowning man drawn out of the flood

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the language thoroughly allegorical and the description ideal: the man nearly overpowered by his foes is shown as one almost drowning. Barnes says the description is taken from the storm, a representation of God’s mighty interposition. Henry reads the shaking earth and hills as men struck with fear, and says David was drawn out of the waters figuratively.
notes.limit: The note does not claim that a storm of this kind came in David’s life, nor that none did; the writers read the storm and the flood as pictures of God’s true rescue of David from his enemies.

cites.quote: From the language being here so thoroughly allegorical, it is clear that we were quite correct in interpreting the description as ideal. He, who is nearly overpowered by his foes, is represented as one engulfed in deep waters and almost drowning.

notes.short: The heavens declare, the skies proclaim
notes.about: The second line says the first again and explains it: the skies proclaim God's glory by showing the work of His hands. They bear witness that they did not come together by chance but were made by Him.

lines.words: The heavens declare the glory of God;
the skies proclaim the work of His hands.

notes.evidence: Calvin says the psalmist repeats one thing twice in this verse, as he often does, and that the second clause only explains the first: the heavens proclaim God's glory by bearing witness that they were not put together by chance but made by the supreme Architect.

notes.short: Voice to all the earth, words to its ends

lines.words: their voice has gone out into all the earth,
their words to the ends of the world.

the commandments of the LORD are radiant, giving light to the eyes.
The fear of the LORD is pure, enduring forever;

Answer us on the day we call.

notes.short: Their descendants, then their offspring: said twice

notes.short: A cry of anguish that still says “my God”
notes.about: The psalm opens not with a statement but a cry. Grief at being forsaken breaks out, yet the sufferer still calls God “my God.” On the cross Jesus cried out these words in a loud voice (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34).

figure.words: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?
figure.means: anguish at being forsaken, from one who still holds to God as his own

notes.limit: The writers hear the cry as Christ's on the cross, some also as David's in his troubles. They differ on how near it comes to despair, but those who weigh it agree the sufferer still holds to God as his own.

figure.words: I am a worm and not a man
figure.means: the speaker made as low as can be, to show how deep his shame and affliction go

notes.short: “My soul”, then “my precious life”: one plea twice

notes.evidence: Barnes takes the works of the Lord as what He does in creation, providence, His laws and His Spirit, and says the sense of the operation of His hands is essentially the same as in the former member of the sentence.

notes.short: From heaven He looks; from His dwelling He gazes
notes.about: Four lines take turns. The third line goes back to the first: the LORD looks down from heaven, and gazes from His dwelling place. The fourth goes back to the second: He sees all the sons of men, all who inhabit the earth.

lines.words: The LORD looks down from heaven;
He sees all the sons of men.
From His dwelling place He gazes
on all who inhabit the earth.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives these verses as four lines with a peculiar artifice in how the sentences are distributed: the latter lines are to be referred in turn to the former.

cites.quote: Those which consist of four lines generally form two regular distichs; but there is sometimes a peculiar artifice to be perceived in the distribution of the sentences ... In both the above passages, the latter members are to be alternately referred to the former.

notes.short: A psalm whose verses follow the Hebrew alphabet
notes.about: In Hebrew each verse begins with the next letter of the alphabet, though no verse begins with the sixth letter. After the last letter comes one more verse, “The LORD redeems His servants,” outside the series, like the last verse of Psalm 25. It may have been added so the psalm ends on a promise.

figure.name: Acrostic
figure.words: I will bless the LORD at all times
figure.means: In Hebrew the verses begin with the alphabet's letters in order, one letter starting none; the last verse, added after the final letter, is outside the series

notes.evidence: Bullinger, under Acrostichion: as in Psalm 25, the sixth letter is omitted and a repeated letter puts verse 22 outside the series. Henry calls it an alphabetical psalm. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) and Barnes note the missing letter and the added verse, which Barnes says makes the verses equal the letters. Benson finds two letters in verse 5 and suggests verse 22 was added to end on a promise.
notes.limit: The pattern shows only in Hebrew, and writers account for its missing letter and its added last verse in different ways.

cites.quote: Here, as in Psa 25:1-22, the sixth letter ו is omitted, the alphabet ending at verse 21; and the פ repeated thus puts verse 22 outside the alphabetical series. Thus far the two Psalms ... are framed on the same model. In this Psalm, with the above exception, there is one letter left for each verse in its order.

notes.short: Contend with them, fight them: one prayer twice
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. He asks the LORD to contend with those who strive with him, and then to fight those who fight him: both lines ask God to take his side against his foes.

lines.words: Contend with my opponents, O LORD;
fight against those who fight against me.

original.note: In Hebrew “contend” and “my opponents” are one word in two forms (riv): the LORD is asked to strive with those who strive with him.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the first line's word means to contend or strive, and that the same word comes again in another form for those who strive against him; of the second line he says the same idea substantially occurs as in the former member of the verse.
notes.limit: The two lines can also be read as different turns of one prayer, the first for his own defence and the second against his enemies.

cites.quote: The original word used here - רוב rûb - means to contend, strive, quarrel; ... The same word is used, in another form, in the other member of the sentence - "with them that strive - יריבי yârı̂ybāy - against me." ... notes.short: Prayers for defence and for attack take turns
notes.about: The lines take turns. The first and third ask the LORD to defend him: to take up his cause, and to take up shield and buckler and come to his aid. The second and fourth ask Him to strike at his enemies: to fight them, and to draw the spear. Each turn takes the prayer further.

lines.words: Contend with my opponents, O LORD;
fight against those who fight against me.
Take up Your shield and buckler; arise and come to my aid.
Draw the spear and javelin against my pursuers;

notes.evidence: Bullinger sets out verses 1 to 3, and then 4 to 8, in alternating lines: prayer for himself, which he calls defensive, in the first, third and fifth, and prayer against his enemies, offensive, in the second, fourth and sixth, the meaning developed further each time.
notes.limit: The turns go on past these four lines: the plea in verse 3 for his soul is for himself again, and verses 4 to 8 are against his enemies. The first two lines can also be read as one plea said twice.

notes.short: Rescue my soul, my precious life, said twice
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. His precious life is his own soul, and the lions are the enemies whose ravages he fears. He asks God to rescue that life from them.

lines.words: Rescue my soul from their ravages
my precious life from these lions

original.note: In Hebrew the word for my precious life means my only one. It can be read as his one life, dear to him, or as his soul left alone, forsaken by his friends.

Albert Barnes (Barnes' Notes) says the darling, in the margin my only one, refers to his own soul or life, the one life he had, and that the lions are his enemies.

notes.short: An alphabet psalm, two verses to each letter
notes.about: In Hebrew this psalm follows the alphabet: verse 1 begins with the first letter, verse 3 with the second, and so on, most letters opening a pair of verses. The pairs can be read as short proverbs on one theme: do not fret at the success of the wicked.

figure.name: Acrostic
figure.words: Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong.
figure.means: In Hebrew verse 1 begins with aleph, the first letter; the next letter opens verse 3, and so on through the psalm.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes calls it an alphabetical psalm whose letters begin every other verse, and names the verses that break the pattern. Joseph Benson says it is alphabetical in every other verse, two verses to each letter. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says it unfolds one thought, not to fret at the prosperity of the ungodly, in short proverbial sayings that follow the order of the alphabet.
notes.limit: A few letters open only one verse. Writers differ on the letter ayin: one finds another letter in its place at verse 29, another finds it inside verse 28, where the verse division runs two sayings together.

cites.quote: This is one of the "alphabetical" psalms ... the successive letters of the alphabet occur at the beginning of every other verse, the first, the third, the fifth, etc. ... In Psa 37:29 the Hebrew letter צ (ts) occurs instead of the Hebrew letter ע (‛); and in Psa 37:7, Psa 37:20, Psa 37:34, the letter introduces only a single verse.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: the Psalm is alphabetical, but not in every verse, as in the two former Psalms we have noticed, namely, the 25th and 34th, but only in every other verse; the plan in this Psalm being to give two verses ... or four hemistics, to each of the Hebrew letters.

The ע strophe begins with לעולם, Psa 37:28

notes.short: The wicked gone, the meek in the land
notes.about: Four lines in two pairs, and the second pair answers the first with its opposite. The wicked will be no more and will not be found; but the meek will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity.

lines.words: Yet a little while, and the wicked will be no more;
though you look for them, they will not be found.
But the meek will inherit the land
and delight in abundant prosperity.

notes.evidence: Lowth says that in these verses the opposition lies between the two halves of a stanza of four lines, the second couplet set against the first.

cites.quote: Yet a little while, and the wicked shall be no more; ... But the meek shall inherit the land; ... In the last example the opposition lies between the two parts of a Stanza of Four lines, the latter Distich being opposed to the former.

notes.short: Nations driven out, Israel planted, in turns
notes.about: The lines can be read as taking turns. The first and third tell what God did to the nations: He drove them out and crushed them. The second and fourth tell what He did for Israel's fathers: He planted them, then sent them out over the land as a vine spreads its branches.

lines.words: With Your hand You drove out the nations
and planted our fathers there
You crushed the peoples
and cast them out

original.note: In Hebrew the last verb, shalach, means to send out, and can be used of a tree or vine sending out its branches.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes (Barnes' Notes) says the last verb may mean the sending out of shoots by a vine, and that the parallelism clearly demands this reading, of the Israelites spread over the land. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the parallel construction makes our fathers the object of the last clause, and that heathen and people both mean the nations driven out.
notes.limit: The BSB, like some other writers, takes the last line of the peoples, cast out of the land. Read that way, the last two lines both tell of the nations, and the lines do not take turns.

cites.quote: How thou didst afflict the people - That is, the people of the land of Canaan ... or it may be used to denote the sending out of shoots or branches by a tree or vine ... and then it would refer here to the Israelites, and would mean that God caused them to increase ... spread them over the land, as a vine spreads, Psa 80:8-11 . The parallelism here clearly demands the latter interpretation.

cites.quote: plantedst them--that is, "our fathers," who are also, from the parallel construction of the last clause, to be regarded as the object of "cast them out," which means--literally, "send" them out, or, "extend them." notes.short: Israel made “a byword among the nations”
notes.about: The psalmist complains that God has made Israel a byword among the nations. They hold Israel up in their taunts as the example of a people brought low and cast off by God, and the peoples laugh it to scorn.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: a byword among the nations
figure.means: Israel’s name, used by the nations as a taunting saying for a people brought to ruin and seemingly abandoned by God

original.note: In Hebrew “byword” is mashal, the word also used for a proverb or a parable.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the Hebrew word means a parable or proverb, and that Israel was made a proverb, pointed to as an instance of divine abandonment and an example of calamity, a warning to all. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a jesting, taunting proverb that holds Israel up as a nation under chastisement. Clarke says they became a proverb among the people for their misery.
notes.limit: The verse does not give the words of the taunt; it says only that Israel itself had become one.

cites.quote: The word rendered "by-word" - משׁל mâshâl - means properly a similitude or parable ... then, a proverb ... The idea here is, that they were made a proverb, or were referred to as a striking instance of the divine abandonment, or as something marked to which the nations might and did refer as an example of calamity, judgment, misfortune, failure; a warning to all.

notes.short: A king’s wedding song read as Christ and His bride
notes.about: The song praises a king for his grace, his victories and his everlasting throne. Then his bride is called to forget her father’s house, and she is led to him with joy. Read as one picture carried through, the King is Christ and the bride His church. Hebrews 1:8-9 applies verses 6 and 7 to the Son.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: Forget your people and your father’s house
figure.means: the church, Christ’s bride, called to leave her old home and belong to Him as her King and Lord

notes.evidence: Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the song is of allegorical, not literal, import: it describes the union of Christ and His Church, the Church portrayed as a bride invited to forsake her home. Henry calls it a song of the holy love between Christ and His church, in which the beauty of the royal bridegroom represents the excellencies of Christ.
notes.limit: Some read the song first as a real king’s wedding, such as Solomon’s, that points ahead to Christ, rather than as an allegory throughout. Either way, Hebrews 1:8-9 applies verses 6 and 7 to the Son.

cites.quote: Maschil-- ... denotes the didactic character of the Psalm; that it gives instruction, the song being of allegorical, and not literal, import. The union and glories of Christ and his Church are described. ... The Church is portrayed in the purity and loveliness of a royally adorned and attended bride, invited to forsake her home and share the honors of her affianced lord.

notes.short: Mouth and heart, wisdom and understanding
notes.about: The second line says the first again from within: the wisdom his mouth will impart is the understanding his heart has pondered. What he is about to teach is weighty, and well thought out before it is spoken.

lines.words: My mouth will impart wisdom
and the meditation of my heart will bring understanding

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls understanding the parallel word to wisdom: profound insight, as the wisdom is weighty wisdom. He says the meditation of the heart stands side by side with the speaking of the mouth. Matthew Henry says the teaching is wisdom and understanding, and that what the psalmist spoke was what his heart had pondered.

Side by side with the speaking of the mouth stands חגוּת לב ... the meditation (lxx μελέτη) of the heart, and in accordance therewith the well-thought-out discourse.

notes.short: The psalmist sets out “my riddle” with the harp
notes.about: The psalmist calls the teaching he is about to sing his riddle: a deep matter that some do not grasp, which he will set forth with the harp. Many read it as the question of what riches are truly worth: the rich trust a false hope, and the poor have a true one.

figure.name: Riddle
figure.words: my riddle
figure.means: the deep matter the psalm goes on to open: what riches are worth, and why they give no true hope

original.note: In Hebrew the word is chidah, from a root meaning to tie a knot: a saying tangled like a knot.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Ænigma, the dark saying: a knotty or intricate saying. Barnes says the point, the value of wealth, was intricate and not well understood, and the psalmist meant to make it plain. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it an involved riddle in its depth, set forth to show the rich their false hope and the poor their true one. Henry says it was a riddle to some.
notes.limit: The riddle lies in the depth of the matter, not in dark wording. The writers differ on how he opens it: two say he makes it plain, one that he sets it forth rather than solves it.

notes.short: Save me by Your name, by Your might

and vindicate me by Your might!

and heals all your diseases,

notes.short: Not always accusing, not angry forever
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. He will not always accuse, and He will not harbor His anger forever: both lines say that His displeasure with His people has an end once His correction has done its work.

lines.words: He will not always accuse us,
nor harbor His anger forever.

original.note: In Hebrew the second line has no word for anger: it says only that He will not keep, natar, forever, and the word anger is rightly supplied.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the second line means the same as the first: He will not always contend with people or show His displeasure, nor cherish hatred once the chastisement has done its work. He adds that the words his anger are supplied by the translators, and not wrongly.

notes.short: As high as, so great; as far as, so far
notes.about: Four lines take turns. The first answers the third: the heavens above the earth, the east from the west. The second answers the fourth: how great His loving devotion is, and how far He has removed our transgressions.

lines.words: For as high as the heavens are above the earth,
so great is His loving devotion for those who fear Him.
As far as the east is from the west,
so far has He removed our transgressions from us.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives these verses as a stanza of four lines that answer one another alternately, the first line to the third and the second to the fourth.

notes.short: Locusts, and “young locusts without number”
notes.about: The second line names the locusts of the first again with another word, and adds that they came without number. The two lines tell one plague, the eighth, the locusts of Exodus 10.

lines.words: He spoke, and the locusts came
young locusts without number.

original.note: In Hebrew the first line's word is arbeh, the locust, and the second's is yeleq, which can mean the grasshopper, set beside it as its parallel.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says verses 34 and 35 tell the eighth plague, the locust of Exodus 10, and that yeleq, which he renders grasshopper, is the parallel word to it here, as another insect's name is in Psalm 78:46.

notes.short: His fathers’ iniquity, his mother’s sin
notes.about: The second line answers the first in other words, most likely to complete the pair: the iniquity of his fathers is answered by the sin of his mother, and being remembered before the LORD by never being blotted out. lines.words: May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the LORD,
and the sin of his mother never be blotted out.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the line on the mother's sin was probably added to complete the parallelism, so that the two lines speak of the sin of his father and his mother.

notes.short: Two halves that answer each other, part by part
notes.about: The verse falls in two halves that answer part by part. Your willing people are seen again arrayed in holy splendor, and Your day of battle is answered by the dew of Your youth. In the second half the picture is dew from the womb of the dawn, fresh and full of strength.

lines.words: Your people shall be willing
on Your day of battle.
Arrayed in holy splendor,
to You belongs the dew of Your youth.

original.note: In Hebrew the first half ends with cheylekha, “Your strength” or army, and the second with yaldutekha, “Your youth”: the two words answer each other.

notes.evidence: Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the dew of Your youth answers the day of Your power in the first clause, and the beauties of holiness belong to the second clause, answering Your people. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the main break after the word for Your army makes its parallel with Your youth stand out, and he takes the holy attire as worn by the people.
notes.limit: Writers differ on the dew of Your youth: the King's own youthful strength, or His host of young men, who come to Him like dew.

notes.short: Each line begins with the next Hebrew letter
notes.about: In Hebrew the psalm's 22 lines begin with the 22 letters of the alphabet in order, two to each of verses 1 to 8 and three to verses 9 and 10. Psalm 112 is built the same way, and the two can be read as a pair: this one praises the LORD for His works, the next blesses “the man who fears the LORD.”

figure.name: Acrostic
figure.words: I will give thanks to the LORD with all my heart
figure.means: the first of 22 lines that, in Hebrew, begin with the letters of the alphabet in order

notes.evidence: Barnes calls it one of the alphabetical psalms: two lettered clauses to each of verses 1 to 8, three to verses 9 and 10. Clarke, calling it acrostic, counts the same 22 lettered parts. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) counts 22 lines with the 22 letters at their head, calls them acrostic lines, and calls Psalms 111 and 112 twins in form and contents.
notes.limit: Why the last two verses have three lines, not two, is left open: one writer says the reason can no longer be found out.

notes.short: Fears the LORD, delights in His commandments
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: the blessed man fears the LORD, and greatly delights in His commandments.

lines.words: Blessed is the man who fears the LORD,
who greatly delights in His commandments.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this verse among his examples of synonymous parallel lines, and says such lines are made of synonymous terms, sometimes three or more and sometimes two.

cites.quote: Blessed is the man, that feareth Jehovah; That greatly delighteth in his commandments. ... In the foregoing examples may be observed the different degrees of Synonymous Parallelism. The Parallel Lines sometimes consist of three or more Synonymous terms; sometimes of two

notes.short: Israel leaves Egypt, told twice in other words
notes.about: Each second line says the line before it again in other words: Israel and the house of Jacob, Egypt and a people of foreign tongue; Judah and Israel, God's sanctuary and His dominion.

lines.words: When Israel departed from Egypt,
the house of Jacob from a people of foreign tongue,
Judah became God’s sanctuary,
and Israel His dominion.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this psalm as his first example of synonymous parallel lines, where the same sentiment is repeated in different but equivalent terms.

notes.short: Eight verses to each Hebrew letter, 22 times
notes.about: In Hebrew the psalm's 176 verses fall into 22 groups of eight, one group for each letter of the alphabet in order, and every verse in a group begins with its letter: verses 1 to 8 with aleph, 9 to 16 with beth, and so on. Many read the pattern as a help to memory.

figure.name: Acrostic
figure.words: Blessed are those whose way is blameless
figure.means: the first verse of the first group; in Hebrew all eight verses here begin with aleph, the first letter

notes.evidence: Barnes calls it the most perfect alphabetical psalm, perhaps arranged to be memorized. Clarke, calling it acrostic, and Benson describe parts of eight verses, each begun with its letter. Calvin says each eight verses begin with their letter to aid memory; Benson sees a memory aid, as the verses are loosely joined. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) counts 22 groups of eight and finds coherence.
notes.limit: Writers differ on how closely the verses are joined: one finds little link from verse to verse, while another finds a train of thought running through the groups.

notes.short: One wish twice: peace and prosperity for the city
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: peace, then prosperity; the walls, then the fortresses. The walls are the ramparts around the city and the fortresses its palaces, so read this way the one wish reaches Jerusalem outside and in.

lines.words: May there be peace within your walls,
and prosperity inside your fortresses.

original.note: In Hebrew peace is shalom and prosperity shalvah, two words alike in sound that echo the name Jerusalem.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) takes the word for palaces as the parallel word to the word for ramparts, so that the wish goes to the city without and within, and notes that the words for peace and prosperity sound alike in Hebrew and both accord with the name of Jerusalem.

notes.short: Eyes on the LORD around servants' eyes
notes.about: The first line lifts the eyes to the One enthroned in heaven, and the last keeps them on the LORD our God. The two lines between give the likeness: servants watching their master's hand, and a maidservant her mistress's.

As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master,
as the eyes of a maidservant look to the hand of her mistress,
so our eyes are on the LORD our God until He shows us mercy.

notes.evidence: Jebb gives these two verses as an example of what he calls the introverted parallelism, in which, he says, the first and last lines are parallel, and so are the second and the next to last.

notes.short: Those who are good are the upright in heart
notes.about: The second line explains the first. Those who are good, for whom the psalmist asks the LORD's goodness, are the upright in heart: people whose hearts are truly right, as God desires, and who are as good as they seem.

lines.words: Do good, O LORD, to those who are good,
and to the upright in heart.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the parallel member of the verse explains who the good are: those uprightly disposed in the bottom of their heart, as God desires. notes.short: House and city: both in vain without the LORD

lines.words: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain;
unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the second half repeats the same idea of dependence in another form: the keeping of a city depends wholly on God. Calvin takes the house to take in the whole order of a family, as the city takes in the whole commonwealth, and says all labor in keeping either is to no purpose unless God gives it success.

in the seas and in all their depths.

made by the hands of men.
They have mouths, but cannot speak;
they have eyes, but cannot see;
they have ears, but cannot hear;
nor is there breath in their mouths.
Those who make them become like them,
as do all who trust in them.

keep watch at the door of my lips.

notes.short: Two lines, one cry, each to the LORD
notes.about: The second line says the first again: I cry aloud, then I lift my voice for mercy. Both lines lay their weight on the words to the LORD, the One he turns to when all others have forsaken him. Saying it twice shows how earnestly he prayed, and he prays aloud.

lines.words: I cry aloud to the LORD;
I lift my voice to the LORD for mercy.

original.note: In Hebrew the two verbs are parallel words: one means to cry out, the other to plead for favor.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the stress of the first two lines rests on the words to the LORD, and that crying out has pleading for favor as its parallel word: an urgent prayer, made not only inwardly but with the voice, by one forsaken by all others. Calvin says the repetition shows that David prayed with earnestness.

cites.quote: The emphasis of the first two lines rests upon אל־ה. Forsaken by all created beings, he confides in Jahve. He turns to Him in pathetic and importunate prayer (זעק, the parallel word being התחנּן, as in Psa 30:9 ), and that not merely inwardly ( Exo 14:15 ), but with his voice

cites.quote: The repetition he makes use of indicates his having prayed with earnestness, so as to be impervious to every assault of temptation.

notes.short: A psalm of praise that runs through the alphabet
notes.about: In Hebrew this psalm runs through the alphabet: each pair of lines opens with the next letter in order, from the first letter to the last. The pattern can be read as marking out the one psalm titled “A Psalm of praise”, and its verses can each stand as a saying of their own.

figure.name: Acrostic
figure.words: I will exalt You
figure.means: In Hebrew this opens a psalm whose pairs of lines begin with the letters of the alphabet in order, from the first letter to the last.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the psalm under Acrostichion: one letter to each verse of two lines marks it as David's special psalm of praise, and a copyist lost the N verse. Barnes: alphabetical, its verses independent sayings. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): each pair's first line has its letter in order; he sees the missing N pair as a poet's freedom. Benson: alphabetical, its verses loosely joined.
notes.limit: Most Hebrew copies lack the last two lines of verse 13, the pair for the letter N, which the BSB includes. Writers differ on why: one says a copyist lost them, another that the psalm never had them.

cites.quote: the Acrostic is perfect, with the exception of the letter Nun ... It has evidently dropped out through the carelessness of some scribe ... The Psalm is “David’s Psalm of praise.” It is the only Psalm that is dignified by this title. It is a special Psalm, therefore, and the Acrostic marks it as such, there being exactly 22 verses, one letter for each verse, and each verse consisting of two lines.

cites.quote: It is an "alphabetical" psalm; that is, each verse begins with a letter of the Hebrew alphabet. ... the composition, as in most of the alphabetical psalms, being made up of independent sentiments suggested in part at least by the necessity of commencing each verse with a particular letter.

notes.short: His word, then His statutes and judgments
notes.about: The second line says the first again and opens it out. His word to Jacob is shown in the second line as His statutes and judgments to Israel: the word He declared to His people unfolds in the laws He made known to them.

lines.words: He declares His word to Jacob,
His statutes and judgments to Israel.

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) points to the plurals of the verse's parallel member and says the word sent to Israel unfolds itself in statutes and judgments. Matthew Henry reads the lines the same way: God showed His word to Jacob, and by that word He made known to them His statutes and judgments.

cites.quote: The Ker דּבריו, occasioned by the plurals of the parallel member of the verse, gives an unlimited indistinct idea. ... The word, which is the medium of God's cosmical rule, is gone forth as a word of salvation to Israel, and, unfolding itself in statutes and judgments, has raised Israel to a legal state

notes.short: From the heavens, in the highest places
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. The heavens of the first line are the highest places of the second, so both lines name the one place where the praise of the LORD is to sound first.

lines.words: Praise the LORD from the heavens;
praise Him in the highest places.

notes.evidence: A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls the heavens and the heights synonymous. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the praise is to sound first from the heavens, in the heights of heaven, and lets the parallel phrase settle how the first line is read. Matthew Henry: the heavens are the heights.

notes.short: Sea creatures to kings, all called to praise
notes.about: The lines are built the same way, a call to praise and then name after name of what is called: sea creatures and depths, lightning and hail, mountains and trees, animals, kings and peoples, young and old, and then let them praise the name of the LORD.

lines.words: Praise the LORD from the earth,
all great sea creatures and ocean depths,
lightning and hail, snow and clouds,
mountains and all hills,
wild animals and all cattle,
kings of the earth and all peoples,
young men and maidens,
Let them praise the name of the LORD,

notes.evidence: Lowth gives these verses as an example of lines that answer each other not word for word but in the shape and build of each sentence and its parts, noun to noun and verb to verb.

cites.quote: similar form of Construction; in which word does not answer to word, and sentence to sentence, as equivalent or opposite; but there is a correspondence and equality between different propositions, in respect of the shape and turn of the whole sentence, and of the constructive parts; such as noun answering to noun, verb to verb, member to member ... Ps. cxlviii. 7-13.
